claims.text: High-temperature stability is governed by competition between high-entropy stabilization and surface-driven segregation or oxidation.
High-entropy stabilization favors retention of a single-phase solid solution.
Differential atomic diffusion and selective oxidation can promote phase segregation or surface oxidation in multi-element nanoparticles.
PtIrOsRhRu or similar near-equiatomic nanoparticles can be synthesized as homogeneous, single-phase structures by freezing in a high-entropy distribution.
Thermal aging under inert and mildly oxidizing atmospheres can be used to distinguish oxidation-associated changes from other high-temperature changes.
The relevant service-temperature windows are 773–1173 K for catalysis and 473–1923 K for thermoelectric use.
The principal structural mediator is the onset of phase segregation and/or growth of a surface oxide layer.
The high surface-to-volume ratio of nanoparticles accelerates atomic diffusion at elevated temperature.
Differences in atomic size and redox potential among constituent elements produce different oxidation tendencies.
Differences in atomic size and redox potential produce different atomic mobilities.
When segregation or oxidation driving forces exceed entropy stabilization, a homogeneous particle decomposes into element-enriched regions or develops oxide patches.
Phase segregation makes the surface elemental distribution non-random.
Nanoparticles that retain a uniform elemental distribution will retain catalytic and thermoelectric performance.
Phase segregation or surface-oxide formation will degrade catalytic or thermoelectric performance relative to the baseline.
Phase segregation or surface oxidation will produce altered diffraction patterns and surface-composition profiles.
Lower-temperature or fully inert aging causes minimal diffusion and oxidation and therefore preserves the initial homogeneous structure and properties.
At temperatures causing melting or sintering, or under extreme oxidation, degradation pathways other than the proposed segregation/oxidation mechanism may dominate.
The relative importance of atomic-size mismatch and redox-potential differences varies with the element set.
Equivalent structural preservation in oxidizing and inert samples, together with no association between structural change and performance loss, would falsify the proposed mechanism.

contradictions.description: The mechanism states that elevated temperature accelerates atomic diffusion, whereas the baseline implies that a fully inert atmosphere itself yields minimal atomic diffusion. Inert gas suppresses oxidation but does not necessarily suppress thermally activated diffusion during high-temperature aging.
